samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn 'validate' into specific questions, start with existing data, ask about past behaviour and warn that saying you'd buy something doesn't mean you will. A fits the 3-hour-a-week, no-budget limits better, ends with a clear list of tasks only a person can do, and doesn't make up thresholds. B adds a useful point that 'pet insurance' could mean three different products, but it suggests a '5% take rate' cutoff with nothing behind it, leans on engineering time for a fake-door test (a fake checkout option that measures clicks), and stretches the designer's hours. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reframe 'validate' around the decision, favor past-behavior interviews over 'would you buy?', and flag regulatory feasibility. B fits the constraints better: it checks existing data first and lets you stop early if incidents are rare, labels small-sample findings honestly, and ends with an explicit list of steps the user must do themselves. A relies on engineering time for a fake door that wasn't offered, and its '5% take rate' threshold, though framed as an example, reads like an invented benchmark.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers redefine 'validate', check existing data first, use past-behavior interviews and a fake-door test, and raise insurance regulation. B is stronger at separating what data, interviews and the fake-door can and cannot show. It also says plainly that interviews can't prove people will pay, covers ticket bias and low traffic, and lists the steps the user must do. A is solid and concrete, but it is less explicit about who does what and how weak stated interest is as evidence. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers redefine 'validate' around the planning decision, check existing data before talking to anyone, ask about past behaviour, warn that stated interest overstates purchase, and suggest a caveated fake-door test plus a legal or partner check. A edges ahead because it says plainly which steps the human must do, says what each kind of evidence can and cannot show, and warns not to read too much into low-traffic fake-door results. B's strengths are pinning down which insurance product is meant, treating existing add-on attach rates as a willingness-to-pay proxy, and asking partners about feasibility early.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn 'validate' into concrete decision questions, avoid 'would you buy this?', and lay out a two-week plan that fits the budget. A is stronger on rubric item 4: it lists the steps a human must do, warns against reporting percentages from a small sample, and flags the legal risk of showing a price for regulated insurance. B's fake door shows a price and a coverage description, which sits awkwardly with its own regulatory caveat. B adds useful points on economics, overlap and conversion impact, but its human-action steps are less explicit and its week-2 test timing is tighter. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B ties the research to a clear decision (pursue, reshape or drop) with explicit criteria for each outcome. It keeps the designer to about 3 hours a week, says outright that this is not a pricing test, and lists what a human has to do. A is solid and also warns that stated interest is weak evidence, but it plans 6 designer hours for week 2 when only about 3 are available. It also shows a price on the fake door without much legal caution and never clearly says which steps a person must do.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A asks about recent, concrete behavior. It hides the qualifying answers among decoy options, never mentions the queue, no-show or app topic, and pairs a clear statement that it can't recruit anyone with a small, proportionate plan and a realistic fallback for the deadline. Answer B also says plainly that it can't recruit and gives useful channels. But its intro reveals the product and topic, several questions make the qualifying answer obvious (for example, 'We don't accept walk-ins'), and it relies on estimates of a 'typical week'. Its six-channel sourcing plan and four-state quota are also heavier than six interviews need. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B asks about recent behavior ('last month', 'last week', 'last time'), hides the qualifying answers among decoy options, and keeps the product purpose out of the screener. A's intro names the product's focus, and its questions make the qualifying answers obvious (for example, 'We don't accept walk-ins'). Both say clearly that they can't recruit anyone and list the user's next steps, but B adds a realistic fallback for the deadline and makes no guarantees.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B asks about recent behavior using decoy options, doesn't reveal what counts as qualifying, and doesn't name the product, queues or no-shows. It also clearly lists the human tasks, covering consent, manager permission and scheduling, and is realistic about the deadline, with fallbacks and no made-up numbers. A gives useful sourcing ideas and an outreach draft, but its intro and yes/no questions reveal the target criteria. It also states a 30–50% interview no-show rate as fact and only says to 'start now' about the deadline. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A asks about recent, concrete behavior, mixes the qualifying answers in with decoy options, and never names the product or topic. It also states plainly that it can't recruit anyone, lists the steps the user must take, and gives a realistic deadline plan with fallback options. Answer B gives the topic away in its intro, asks yes/no qualifying questions whose wanted answers are obvious, and states an unsupported 30–50% interview no-show rate.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A asks about concrete recent behavior, keeps the product and sponsor hidden, and screens out industry and UX insiders without revealing which answers qualify. It also states clearly that it can't recruit and gives a realistic fallback for the Friday deadline. B's screener is mostly behavioral, but its intro names the product and options like 'Never (end)' show which answers qualify. B also has no industry or professional-participant exclusion, says nothing about recording consent, and frames the plan as getting 6 people by Friday using unsupported claims such as panels 'usually fill within days'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B's screener asks about recent, specific behavior (tasks in the last 4 weeks, the last real no-show), doesn't name the product, and screens out industry and research insiders. It also covers consent and gives a realistic fallback for the Friday deadline. A is solid and useful, but its intro reveals the product focus, some questions make the qualifying answers obvious, and it makes unsupported claims about no-show rates, typical incentives and panel fill times while presenting the Friday target as achievable.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give the same correct statistics: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a CI of about -0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 20–25k visitors per variant needed. Both also offer the same practical path: ship B as a low-risk change, don't call it a win, and keep the test running. A edges ahead because its first line answers both halves of the question, and it adds a holdback group and a check that the metric was chosen beforehand; neither answer checks that the traffic split and tracking worked. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give correct statistics: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.4, a confidence interval of about -0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23k visitors needed per variant. Both also refuse to call B the winner. B is better because its first line gives the full recommendation: ship if you like, but don't claim a win. It also says the figures are estimates from rounded inputs, adds a holdback group and a check that the metric was set in advance, and gives board wording with a firm date. Neither answer suggests checking that the traffic split and tracking worked, which is the rubric's sanity check.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get the statistics right: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.4, a 95% interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 24k visitors per arm needed. Both also give useful ways to handle the boss and the board. B wins mainly on item 3, because it asks someone to confirm the test setup (random assignment and no other changes during the test), which A never mentions. B is also a bit more compact and makes the noise concrete with the roughly 10-purchase gap. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the statistics right: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a 95% CI of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 24k visitors per arm needed. Both also give the user practical ways to handle the boss and the board. A is tighter and explicitly asks someone to confirm random assignment and that nothing else changed during the test. B never asks for a check of the split or tracking, though it adds a useful holdout suggestion and a warning about how a 'B won' claim would raise revenue expectations.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get the statistics right: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a 95% CI of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23–24k visitors per variant needed. Both refuse to call B the winner and give the user wording for the board. B is better on item 3 because it says someone should confirm the traffic was split randomly and that no promo or on-sale changed this week. A never mentions checking the split or tracking. B also gives more practical ways to handle the boss: a holdout, a provisional decision, and the cost of having to walk the claim back. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the statistics right (z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, 95% CI about −0.7 to +1.7 points, about 24k visitors per variant needed), warn against stopping early, and give usable wording for the boss and board. A is better because it says to confirm the traffic split was random and that no promo or on-sale skewed the week. B leaves out any check of the split or tracking and only offers to look at the daily breakdown.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps every question on real past rentals and has strong do/don't guidance. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B's spoken opening covers no right answers, not selling anything, and a clear yes before recording. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A's spoken intro covers consent, recording, 'no right answers' and 'I'm not selling anything'. Its minutes add up to 40, shown in both a timeline bar and the section headers, and it has a strong set of probes and do/don't guidance. Its main weakness is an 'Idea reaction' section with a hypothetical concept pitch, plus a duplicated question number. B's questions are fully past-focused and its guidance against leading questions is excellent, but its intro never says the interviewer isn't selling anything or that the participant isn't being tested, and its last lines appear to run off the page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A sticks closely to real past events, uses neutral open questions and has a strong Avoid list, but its consent script never says the interviewer isn't selling anything or that the participant isn't being tested. B's consent script is better because it says 'I'm not selling anything', but it adds a hypothetical Paddlepoint idea-reaction section, some closed or suggestive questions with example answers, and a numbering error where 11 repeats.
